messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 21
- Gender: Female
- Ethnicity: North American
- Relationship Status: Single
- Occupation: Electrician
- Trauma Type: Life-threatening motor vehicle collision
- Pcl5: 35

She is 21, single, and works as an electrician, a job she has grown into with pride because it asks her to be steady, practical, and unafraid of tight spaces, ladders, and sharp attention. Before the accident, she describes herself as the kind of person who likes motion and competence: she gets up early, packs her tools, and goes where the work is. She is used to being on construction sites where people call out measurements and joke through the noise, and she likes that her hands know what to do even when her thoughts are busy.

The collision changes that sense of herself in a single violent moment. She is driving when another vehicle strikes her, and the crash is so severe that she experiences it as a kind of rupture, as if the world tears open and she is suddenly no longer inside ordinary time. She remembers metal, sound, and a sensation of helplessness that feels larger than fear. In the aftermath, she is aware of the danger before she is fully aware of pain. Her body feels foreign, and she is struck by the thought that she might die there, trapped and unable to do anything useful. That thought lingers with unusual force because she has always been someone who fixes things.

In the days after, she moves through the world as if she is still waiting for the crash to end. She startles at sudden braking, at honking horns, at the backfire of a truck in the distance. She does not realize at first how often her body is bracing until she notices how tightly she holds the steering wheel. When she gets into a vehicle, she scans the road obsessively, trying to predict every possible threat. Riding as a passenger is worse. She feels exposed, unable to control speed or distance, and she keeps her eyes locked ahead, jaw clenched, waiting for impact. Even minor traffic feels loaded with danger.

She begins to have intrusive recollections that arrive without warning. Sometimes a flash of headlights is enough to pull her back into the collision for a second, and her chest tightens before she can tell herself she is safe. At night, her sleep is interrupted by dreams in which she is again inside the wreck, trying to move but unable to get free. She wakes disoriented and sweaty, with her heart racing, then lies awake listening to the house and replaying the sequence of the crash, as though if she thinks through it carefully enough she can prevent it from happening again. Instead of feeling reassured, she becomes more alert, more exhausted, and more certain that danger is always just ahead.

At work, she is determined not to appear shaken, but the accident follows her there too. On site, loud metallic bangs make her flinch. A sudden loss of footing on a ladder can send a wave of panic through her body, and she has to pause and press a hand against the wall until the dizziness passes. She notices that she has become more cautious than she used to be, avoiding unfamiliar routes, leaving extra time for every drive, and sometimes turning down social plans if they involve highway traffic or late-night travel. She tells herself she is being sensible, but there is also grief in how much smaller her world has become.

Emotionally, she feels changed in ways that are hard to describe to other people. She is more irritable and quicker to snap, especially when she is tired. She is also more easily overwhelmed by crowded, noisy places. At times she feels detached from people around her, as if she is present but not fully connected. She misses the version of herself who trusted her body and moved through the day without constant calculation. Now she watches for exits, checks mirrors repeatedly, and notices her pulse rising in situations that used to feel ordinary. Even when nothing bad is happening, she carries the uneasy sense that something could happen at any moment.

Over time, she learns that she can continue to function, but not without cost. She keeps showing up for work, keeps her tools organized, keeps driving, yet everything takes more effort than it once did. The accident sits in the background of nearly every day, shaping how she drives, how she sleeps, how she responds to noise and speed and the feel of being trapped. She speaks about the crash with a kind of flatness at first, then with visible strain when she reaches the part where she remembers how close she felt to dying. Even now, she lives with the impression that the world is less predictable than it was before, and that the body she relies on so much can no longer be taken for granted.
